cse-2019-cs-35.approach: Read $\varphi$ as "for every prime $x$ there is a prime $w > x$" (the antecedent says $x$ has only the divisors $1$ and $x$). Then a set satisfies $\varphi$ exactly when it has no largest prime, so test each set for a largest prime.

steps.title: Translate the formula
steps.body:
Antecedent $\forall z\,(z\mid x \Rightarrow z = x \lor z = 1)$: "$x$ is prime" (only divisors $1$ and itself). Consequent $\exists w\,(w > x) \land (\forall z\, z\mid w \Rightarrow w = z \lor z = 1)$: "there is a prime $w$ larger than $x$".

So $\varphi \equiv$ "every prime in the domain has a larger prime in the domain".

steps.title: S1 = {1, …, 100}
steps.body: Take $x = 97$ (prime). The next prime is $101 \notin S_1$, and $98, 99, 100$ are composite. No $w$ exists, so $\varphi$ is **false** on $S_1$.

steps.title: S2 and S3
steps.body: There are infinitely many primes (Euclid), and every positive prime lies in both $S_2$ and $S_3$. For any prime $x$ a larger prime $w$ always exists in the domain, so $\varphi$ is **true** on $S_2$ and on $S_3$ (intended reading, with primes taken as positive).

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: $\varphi$ holds on $S_2$ and $S_3$ only → **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Includes S1, which fails at $x = 97$ (no larger prime ≤ 100).
Includes S1, which fails; also omits S2, which satisfies $\varphi$.
Both infinite sets contain infinitely many primes, so every prime has a larger one.
S1 is finite with largest prime 97, so it does not satisfy $\varphi$.

pitfalls: Testing $x = 100$ in S1: it is not prime, so the implication is vacuously true there — the failing witness is the largest prime 97.
Over-reading S3 with negative divisors ($-1 \mid w$ for every $w$) — the intended reading uses the usual (positive) notion of a prime.
cse-2019-cs-35.verification: Largest prime ≤ 100 is 97 (99 = 9·11, 98 and 100 even), confirming S1 fails; S2/S3 contain all primes.

steps.title: L → L₁ , id

steps.title: Median of the medians

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $O(n^2) + O(n) = O(n^2)$ → **(C)**. It is also a lower bound in spirit: every one of the $n^2$ elements must be read.

cse-2019-cs-38.approach: Both conditions are standard sufficient conditions for MST uniqueness: distinct weights imply a unique light edge in every cut, and a unique light edge in every cut forces every MST to contain exactly those edges.

steps.title: Statement II
steps.body: Suppose two different MSTs $T_1 \ne T_2$. Take an edge $e \in T_1 \setminus T_2$; removing it splits $T_1$ into a cut. $T_2$ has some edge $f$ crossing that cut. If the cut has a unique minimum edge, swapping either gives a strictly lighter spanning tree for whichever tree does not use it — contradiction. Hence the MST is unique. **True.**

steps.title: Statement I
steps.body: If all edge weights are distinct, every cut certainly has a unique minimum-weight crossing edge, so II applies. **True.**

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Both I and II are true → **(C)**. (The converse of I is false: a graph can have equal weights and still a unique MST.)

optionAnalysis.reason: II is also true — it is the cut-based uniqueness condition.
I is a special case of II, so it is true as well.
Distinct weights ⇒ unique light edge per cut ⇒ unique MST.
Both are well-known sufficient conditions.

cse-2019-cs-38.verification: I ⇒ II (distinct weights give unique cut minima), and II ⇒ uniqueness by the exchange argument.

cse-2019-cs-39.approach: Only $p$ and $q$ can finish immediately (they need nothing more). After they release, exactly $X_p + X_q$ instances are free. If that is smaller than every other process's maximum remaining need, no one else can be guaranteed to finish.

steps.title: Free instances after p and q
steps.body: All instances are in use, so initially available $= 0$. $p$ and $q$ have $Y = 0$ and finish, releasing $X_p + X_q$ instances. Available becomes $X_p + X_q$.

steps.title: Can any other process proceed?
steps.body: Process $k$ (worst case) needs $Y_k$ more. If $X_p + X_q < Y_k$ for **every** $k \ne p, q$, i.e. $X_p + X_q < \min_k Y_k$, no other process can be satisfied, so none can complete.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: So the guarantee is $X_p + X_q < \min\{Y_k \mid k \ne p, q\}$, condition **(A)**. Comparing with the max (B) or with only one of $X_p, X_q$ (C, D) does not cover every other process.

answer.value: Xp + Xq < Min{Yk | k ≠ p, q}

optionAnalysis.reason: Released instances are less than the smallest outstanding need, so nobody can be served.
Below the max only blocks the neediest process; one with smaller $Y_k$ may still finish.
If even one of $X_p, X_q$ covers the smallest need, that process can finish — the opposite of what is asked.
Gives no guarantee: e.g. $X_p + X_q$ may still be ≥ some $Y_k$.

cse-2019-cs-39.verification: Example: $X_p = X_q = 1$, others need $Y_k \ge 3$; available 2 < 3, all others stuck — consistent with A.

cse-2019-cs-40.approach: Check each statement against heap structure and known lower bounds: III works because an in-order traversal gives a sorted array (already a heap when reversed), while IV would sort the heap and so needs $\Omega(n\log n)$.

steps.title: I and II
steps.body:
**I:** An internal node is larger than its children, so the minimum cannot be internal — it is at a leaf. True.

**II:** The second largest element is smaller only than the root; its parent must be larger than it, so its parent is the root. True.

steps.title: III — BST to max-heap
steps.body: In-order traversal of a BST gives the keys in sorted order in $\Theta(n)$; a descending sorted array is a valid max-heap (or run build-heap, $O(n)$). True.

steps.title: IV — max-heap to BST
steps.body: A BST's in-order traversal gives sorted output in $O(n)$, so building a BST from a heap in $\Theta(n)$ would sort in $O(n)$ by comparisons — impossible ($\Omega(n\log n)$). False.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: I, II and III → **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: I, II, III true; IV false.
IV would imply linear-time comparison sorting.
Omits II (true) and includes IV (false).
Omits I (true) and includes IV (false).

cse-2019-cs-40.verification: Lower-bound argument for IV is standard; I/II follow directly from the heap order property.

cse-2019-cs-41.approach: Simulate SRTF for the first three processes (independent of Z), compute their waiting times, then find which Z makes the total waiting time $4 \times 1 = 4$ ms.

steps.title: Up to t = 4
steps.body: $t=0$: P1 runs. $t=1$: P2 arrives (burst 1) < P1 remaining 2 → preempt, P2 runs 1–2. $t=2$: P1 resumes (remaining 2). $t=3$: P3 arrives with 3 > 1 remaining → P1 continues and finishes at $t=4$.

steps.title: Waiting so far
steps.body: P1: $4 - 0 - 3 = 1$. P2: $2 - 1 - 1 = 0$. Required total: $4 \times 1 = 4$, so P3 + P4 must wait $4 - 1 = 3$ ms.

steps.title: Case Z < 3
steps.body: At $t=4$, P4 (Z) beats P3 (3): P4 runs $4$ to $4+Z$, waiting 0. P3 runs $4+Z$ to $7+Z$, waiting $(7+Z) - 3 - 3 = 1 + Z$. Need $1 + Z = 3 \Rightarrow Z = 2$.

steps.title: Case Z ≥ 3 rules out
steps.body: P3 (3) runs first 4–7, waiting 1; P4 then waits $7 - 4 = 3$. Total $1 + 3 = 4 \ne 3$. So $Z = 2$ is the only solution.

pitfalls: Forgetting that P2 preempts P1 at $t = 1$.
Using burst time instead of arrival when computing P3's waiting time.
cse-2019-cs-41.verification: With Z = 2: waits are 1, 0, 3, 0 → total 4 → average 1 ms ✓.

cse-2019-cs-42.approach: Pointers per block = block size / address size; max file size = (direct + single-indirect + double-indirect data blocks) × block size.

steps.title: Data blocks addressable

steps.title: Size
steps.body: $1049612 \times 4\,\text{KB} = 48\,\text{KB} + 4\,\text{MB} + 4\,\text{GB} \approx 4.0039\,\text{GB} \approx \mathbf{4.0}$ GB.

pitfalls: Using 32-bit addresses as a 4 GB cap on *disk* rather than counting blocks — the answer is still ≈ 4.0 GB here.
cse-2019-cs-42.verification: Dominant term $2^{20} \times 2^{12} = 2^{32}$ B = 4 GB; the rest adds only ≈ 4 MB.

cse-2019-cs-43.approach: Advance the dot over $\langle$ in the only item of $I_0$ that has $\bullet\langle$, then take the closure (add items for $L$, then for $S$).

steps.title: Items of I₀
steps.body: $I_0 = \{ S' \to \bullet S,\; S \to \bullet\langle L\rangle,\; S \to \bullet id \}$.

steps.title: Kernel of GOTO(I₀, ⟨)
steps.body: Only $S \to \bullet\langle L \rangle$ moves: kernel $S \to \langle \bullet L \rangle$.

steps.title: Closure
steps.body:
Dot before $L$: add $L \to \bullet L,S$ and $L \to \bullet S$. Dot before $S$: add $S \to \bullet\langle L\rangle$ and $S \to \bullet id$.

Items: $S \to \langle\bullet L\rangle$, $L \to \bullet L,S$, $L \to \bullet S$, $S \to \bullet\langle L\rangle$, $S \to \bullet id$ → **5**.

cse-2019-cs-48.approach: The DFA only needs to track the current product $\pi$ of the prefix, an element of the permutation group $S_5$. All $5! = 120$ products are reachable and pairwise distinguishable, so the minimum DFA has 120 states.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: States = permutations of $\{1..5\}$; start and accepting state = $id$; on symbol $\sigma$ go from $g$ to $g\circ\sigma$. That DFA has $5! = 120$ states and accepts $L$.

steps.title: All states needed
steps.body: Each permutation is a one-letter string, so all 120 states are reachable. For prefixes $x, y$ with $\pi(x) = g \ne h = \pi(y)$, append the single symbol $g^{-1}$: $\pi(xg^{-1}) = id$ but $\pi(yg^{-1}) = hg^{-1} \ne id$. So they are distinguishable.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: No dead state is needed (every element has an inverse), so the minimum is **120**.

pitfalls: Adding a dead state — it would never be reached, because any product can be brought back to $id$.

cse-2019-cs-50.approach: Simplify with a K-map: the minterms give $f = BD + \bar B\bar D = B \odot D$ (XNOR). Write it as a product of sums, which maps directly to a two-level NOR–NOR circuit.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.body: With $f(A,B,C,D)$: minterms $0,2,8,10$ have $B = 0, D = 0$ → $\bar B\bar D$; minterms $5,7,13,15$ have $B = 1, D = 1$ → $BD$. So $f = BD + \bar B\bar D$.

steps.title: POS form
steps.body: $f = (\bar B + D)(B + \bar D)$ (check: expanding gives $\bar B B + \bar B\bar D + BD + D\bar D = BD + \bar B\bar D$).

steps.title: NOR–NOR
steps.body: $f = \text{NOR}\big(\text{NOR}(\bar B, D),\ \text{NOR}(B, \bar D)\big)$, since $\overline{\overline{(x+y)} + \overline{(u+v)}} = (x+y)(u+v)$. Complements are available, so **3** gates. One or two NOR gates realise only single sums or a product of one sum with literals, not XNOR.
